Harold Godwinson. Around ten twenty-two to ten sixty-six, Harold Godwinson was the last Anglo-Saxon king of England, ruling for only nine months before his death at the Battle of Hastings in ten sixty-six. His defeat by William the Conqueror and the Norman invasion marked the end of Anglo-Saxon rule and initiated the profound cultural and political transformation that shaped medieval and modern England.

Harold was born into the powerful Godwin family, the dominant English aristocracy under Edward the Confessor. He rose to become Earl of Wessex and the most influential magnate in the kingdom. On his deathbed in January ten sixty-six, King Edward the Confessor named Harold as his successor, though the exact circumstances were disputed. Harold was crowned king and claimed legitimate succession to the English throne.

Multiple claimants contested this succession. William, Duke of Normandy claimed Edward had once promised him the throne. Harald Hardrada, the Norwegian king, also pressed claims. Harold faced simultaneous threats from three directions. He won a decisive victory over Harald Hardrada and the Earls of Mercia and Northumbria at Stamford Bridge on September twenty-fifth, ten sixty-six, reportedly killing the Norwegian king. This triumph exhausted Harold's army just as William's invasion fleet landed in Sussex.

At the Battle of Hastings on October fourteenth, ten sixty-six, Harold's forces faced Norman knights and archers. Harold was killed in battle, legend says by an arrow through his eye. His army was routed, and the Norman conquest of England began. His death and defeat severed Anglo-Saxon royal lineage. The Norman dynasty under William established a new nobility, feudal system, and cultural synthesis of Norman-French and Anglo-Saxon elements that would define England's future.
